questions.title: What should a Go developer know about SQL transactions in Go
questions.direct_answer: A SQL transaction groups statements into one database unit of work. In Go, `BeginTx` returns `*sql.Tx`; statements run through that value until `Commit` makes the changes durable or `Rollback` abandons them. The transaction is bound to one database connection. Reads and writes inside it see the database's transaction rules and isolation level, so using `db.QueryContext` halfway through would run outside that transaction.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A SQL transaction groups statements into one database unit of work. In Go, `BeginTx` returns `*sql.Tx`; statements run through that value until `Commit` makes the changes durable or `Rollback` abandons them.

The transaction is bound to one database connection. Reads and writes inside it see the database's transaction rules and isolation level, so using `db.QueryContext` halfway through would run outside that transaction.

For example, a money transfer debits one account and credits another. Both updates must run through the same `*sql.Tx`; if the credit fails, rollback prevents the database from keeping only the debit.

A database transaction does not automatically roll back an email, HTTP call, or message already sent to another system. Cross-system workflows need patterns such as an outbox, idempotency, compensation, or a carefully designed distributed protocol.

Use a transaction when several database changes must succeed or fail together, or when a read-modify-write decision needs a defined isolation boundary. Keep the transaction short and avoid slow network calls while it holds database resources.

sections.title: The core model: SQL transactions in Go
sections.content:
SQL transactions in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

Atomicity is the central promise: either the database accepts all changes in the unit or none of them. Go does not infer that unit from function boundaries; code must begin a transaction and send each relevant statement through the returned `*sql.Tx`. A deferred rollback is a convenient safety net because rollback after a successful commit returns an error but causes no database change. Commit itself can fail, so success is not known until its result is checked. Isolation is separate from atomicity. Concurrent transactions may still observe or conflict with one another according to the database and requested level. Correct code protects a business invariant—for example, total transferred money—using suitable statements, constraints, locks, or retry logic. The transaction should also remain local to database work. Holding it open while calling another service increases lock time and still cannot make that remote side effect atomic.
